question: when do i actually have to start paying my student loans back after graduation?
answer: For Direct Subsidized and Unsubsidized Loans, you get a six-month grace period that starts the day after you graduate, leave school or drop below half-time enrollment. Repayment begins the day after the grace period ends, and your first payment is due within 60 days of that. Your loan servicer will contact you with your exact due date, so make sure it has your current email and address.

question: I used my grace period, then went back to school and dropped out again. Do I get another six months?
answer: Usually not. The grace period on a Direct Subsidized or Unsubsidized Loan only starts if it hasn't already been used up, so once you've used the full six months it doesn't reset when you re-enroll and leave again. While you're back in school at least half-time you can generally get an in-school deferment, but when you leave, repayment starts without a new grace period. Check your loan status in your StudentAid.gov account or ask your servicer.

question: Does interest build up on my loans during the grace period?
answer: It depends on the loan type. On Direct Unsubsidized Loans, interest keeps accruing during school and the grace period, and you can pay it or let it be added to your principal later. On Direct Subsidized Loans you generally aren't charged interest during the grace period, with a narrow exception for some older subsidized loans. Paying the unsubsidized interest before repayment starts keeps your balance from growing.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.207 (eCFR)
sources.section: (b)-(c) Interest during in-school and grace periods

question: Do Parent PLUS loans have a grace period like my kid's loans do?
answer: Not in the same way. Repayment on a Direct PLUS Loan begins once it's fully disbursed, and interest starts on the day of the first disbursement. A parent borrower can ask for a deferment while the student is enrolled at least half-time and for six months after the student leaves half-time enrollment, but the parent has to request it. Contact the loan servicer to set that up, and keep in mind interest continues to accrue during the deferment.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.204 (eCFR)
sources.section: (c) Direct PLUS in-school and post-enrollment deferment

question: Grad student with a Grad PLUS loan - is there any break after I finish before payments start?
answer: Yes, through a deferment rather than a grace period. A student PLUS borrower can get a deferment during the six months after they stop being enrolled at least half-time, which works much like a grace period. Interest keeps accruing on PLUS loans during that time. Ask your servicer to confirm the deferment is on your account before your first bill.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.204 (eCFR)
sources.section: (c) Post-enrollment deferment for student PLUS borrowers

question: My grace period started and then my Reserve unit got called to active duty. Do I lose the rest of it?
answer: No. If you're a member of a reserve component called or ordered to active duty for more than 30 days, that period, plus the time needed to re-enroll at the next regular enrollment period, can be excluded from your grace period. If you were already in your grace period when you were called up, you get a full six-month grace period after the excluded period ends. Tell your loan servicer about the orders so it can apply the rule.

question: can i pay on my student loan while im still in college or do i have to wait?
answer: You can pay any time. Federal rules let you prepay all or part of a Direct Loan at any time without a penalty. Paying while you're in school, especially the interest on unsubsidized loans, can lower the total amount you repay. Log in to your StudentAid.gov account to see who your servicer is, then make payments through the servicer.

sources.title: Student Loan Repayment Checklist (Federal Student Aid, PDF)

question: If I send extra money to my loan servicer, does it go to the principal?
answer: Not first. On most plans, a payment goes first to any fees or collection costs, then to outstanding interest, then to principal. On income-based plans, including the Repayment Assistance Plan, it goes to accrued interest first, then fees, then principal. If you pay at least a full monthly amount extra, the servicer will move your next due date unless you ask it not to, so tell your servicer how you want extra payments handled.

question: What is the new Repayment Assistance Plan everyone's talking about?
answer: The Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) is a new income-driven plan available starting July 1, 2026. Your yearly payment is 1% to 10% of your adjusted gross income depending on how much you earn, it's divided by 12, and then it's reduced by $50 a month for each dependent you claim on your federal tax return. The minimum payment is $10 a month. You can apply through your StudentAid.gov account, and consenting to have your tax information pulled from the IRS makes it faster.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: The Trump Administration Is Simplifying Student Loan Repayment

question: is there a $0 payment option on RAP if i'm not making much?
answer: No. Under RAP, if your adjusted gross income is $10,000 or less your yearly amount is set at $120, and any monthly payment that would fall below $10 is set at $10. So the lowest regular RAP payment is $10 a month, unlike the older income-driven plans, where payments could be $0. If even that's not manageable, ask your servicer about deferment or forbearance.

question: On RAP, what happens if my payment doesn't even cover the interest?
answer: If you make your full RAP payment on time and it doesn't cover the interest that accrued that month, the unpaid interest isn't charged to you. RAP also has a principal match: if an on-time payment reduces your principal by less than $50, the Department reduces your principal further, up to $50 for that month. These benefits depend on on-time payments, so set up autopay or reminders with your servicer.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: The Trump Administration Is Simplifying Student Loan Repayment

question: Does RAP ever forgive what's left of the loan?
answer: Yes, but it takes a long time. Under RAP, any remaining balance can be forgiven after you've made 360 qualifying monthly payments, which is at least 30 years. Qualifying payments include on-time RAP payments, certain payments under other plans and certain months of deferment or forbearance. Your servicer tracks the count, and you can check your progress in your StudentAid.gov account.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: The Trump Administration Is Simplifying Student Loan Repayment

question: Which loans can go on the Repayment Assistance Plan?
answer: RAP covers Direct Subsidized Loans, Direct Unsubsidized Loans, Direct PLUS Loans made to graduate or professional students, and Direct Consolidation Loans that didn't repay a parent PLUS loan. Parent PLUS loans, and consolidation loans that repaid a parent PLUS loan, can't be repaid under RAP. Your servicer can tell you which of your loans qualify.

question: How long is the new standard repayment plan for loans taken out this year?
answer: For Direct Loans made on or after July 1, 2026, the standard plan is a Tiered Standard plan with fixed payments, and the term depends on your total balance when you enter repayment. It's 10 years if you owe less than $25,000, 15 years for $25,000 to under $50,000, 20 years for $50,000 to under $100,000, and 25 years for $100,000 or more. Payments are at least $50 a month unless your balance is smaller than that.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: The Trump Administration Is Simplifying Student Loan Repayment

question: I'm a freshman borrowing for the first time in fall 2026. What repayment plans will I be able to choose from?
answer: Federal Direct Loans made on or after July 1, 2026 can be repaid under two plans: the Tiered Standard plan, with fixed payments over 10 to 25 years depending on what you owe, or the income-based Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP). The older plans, such as IBR, PAYE, ICR, and the old graduated and extended plans, aren't available for loans made on or after that date. You'll choose a plan with your servicer before repayment begins.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.208 (eCFR)
sources.section: (c)(1) Plans for loans made on or after July 1, 2026

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.209 (eCFR)
sources.section: (d)(5) Only loans made before July 1, 2026 may use PAYE, IBR, ICR

sources.title: Fact Sheet: The Trump Administration Is Simplifying Student Loan Repayment

question: I already have loans from before July 2026. If I take out another loan now, do I lose my old repayment options?
answer: It can change your options, so check before you borrow. Under the current regulations, loans made before July 1, 2026 can still be repaid under IBR, but loans made on or after that date can't. The older standard, graduated and extended plans are only for borrowers who haven't received a Direct Loan on or after July 1, 2026, and a borrower with both old and new loans uses the Tiered Standard plan. These rules are new and complicated, so ask your servicer how a new loan would affect each of your existing loans before you accept it.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.208 (eCFR)
sources.section: (b)(1), (b)(8) Borrowers with loans before and after July 1, 2026

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.209 (eCFR)
sources.section: (d)(5) Loans eligible for IBR, PAYE, ICR

question: Is the SAVE plan over? What do people on SAVE have to do now?
answer: Yes. In 2026 a federal court approved a settlement between the Department of Education and the State of Missouri that ended the SAVE plan, and the Department isn't enrolling new borrowers or approving pending SAVE applications. Starting July 1, 2026, servicers began sending SAVE borrowers notices giving them at least 90 days to move to a legal plan, such as an income-driven plan, the Repayment Assistance Plan or the Tiered Standard plan. Your servicer's notice gives your specific deadline, and you can switch any time before it through your StudentAid.gov account or your servicer.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Education Announces Next Steps for Borrowers Enrolled in the Unlawful SAVE Plan
sources.section: Settlement; next steps for SAVE borrowers

question: What happens if I'm on SAVE and I just ignore the letter about switching plans?
answer: If you don't choose a new plan within the 90-day window your servicer gives you, the Department says you'll be automatically placed in either the Standard Repayment Plan or the Tiered Standard plan. Those are fixed-payment plans, so your payment could be much higher than an income-based one. It's better to choose a plan before your deadline; you can apply for an income-driven plan or RAP through your StudentAid.gov account.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Education Announces Next Steps for Borrowers Enrolled in the Unlawful SAVE Plan

question: I'm on PAYE. Do I have to leave it, and by when?
answer: Yes, eventually. PAYE and ICR are being phased out, and borrowers repaying under them must choose another plan before July 1, 2028, with options including RAP, the Tiered Standard plan, or IBR. If you don't choose by then, loans eligible for RAP are moved to RAP and the rest go to IBR. You can switch earlier by applying through your StudentAid.gov account or contacting your servicer.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: The Trump Administration Is Simplifying Student Loan Repayment

question: Is IBR still a thing after all these changes?
answer: Yes, for older loans. Under the current rules, Direct Loans made before July 1, 2026 can still be repaid under Income-Based Repayment, and IBR is one of the plans PAYE, ICR and SAVE borrowers can move to. Loans made on or after July 1, 2026 can't use IBR; they're limited to the Tiered Standard plan and RAP. Your servicer can confirm which of your loans are IBR-eligible.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: The Trump Administration Is Simplifying Student Loan Repayment

question: Can I still sign up for SAVE if I apply now?
answer: No. Under the court-approved settlement, the Department of Education isn't enrolling new borrowers in SAVE and is denying pending SAVE applications. If you need a payment based on your income, look at the Repayment Assistance Plan or, if your loans qualify, Income-Based Repayment. You can compare and apply through your StudentAid.gov account or ask your servicer.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Education Announces Next Steps for Borrowers Enrolled in the Unlawful SAVE Plan

question: My parents are taking out a Parent PLUS loan for my sophomore year. Can they use the income-based RAP plan to repay it?
answer: No. Parent PLUS loans are excluded from the Repayment Assistance Plan. A Parent PLUS loan made on or after July 1, 2026 is repaid under the Tiered Standard plan, with fixed payments over 10 to 25 years depending on the balance. Rules for older Parent PLUS loans and Parent PLUS consolidation loans are different and have changed recently, so your parents should ask their servicer which plans apply to their loans.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.209 (eCFR)
sources.section: (b)(8) Excepted PLUS loan; (d)(4) RAP eligible loans

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.208 (eCFR)
sources.section: (c)(1) Tiered Standard for loans made on or after July 1, 2026

question: My mom consolidated her old Parent PLUS loans and is on ICR. Can she stay on it?
answer: Not permanently. Under the current regulations, a borrower can choose ICR for a consolidation loan that repaid a parent PLUS loan only through June 30, 2028, and that option isn't available to a borrower who has received a Direct Loan on or after July 1, 2026. What happens after 2028 for these loans depends on detailed transition rules, so she should ask her servicer what her options will be and when she has to choose.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.209 (eCFR)
sources.section: (c)(5) ICR for consolidation loans that repaid parent PLUS loans

question: what's the difference between deferment and forbearance?
answer: Both let you temporarily stop or reduce payments, but they treat interest differently. During a deferment, you generally aren't charged interest on Direct Subsidized Loans, but interest keeps accruing on unsubsidized and PLUS loans. During a forbearance, interest accrues on all loan types. Deferments are for specific situations like being in school or serving in the military, while forbearance is for other hardships; ask your servicer which one you qualify for.

question: Can I still get an unemployment deferment if I can't find a job after graduating?
answer: It depends on when your loans were disbursed. For loans disbursed before July 1, 2027, unemployment and economic hardship deferments are still available, each capped at three years in total. For loans disbursed on or after July 1, 2027, those two deferments aren't available at all. If you're struggling, an income-based plan like RAP may give you a lower payment; ask your servicer which options fit your loans.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.204 (eCFR)
sources.section: Unemployment and economic hardship deferment limits

sources.title: Reimagining and Improving Student Education; Federal Student Loan Program Final Regulations (Federal Register, May 1, 2026)

question: How long can I put my loans in forbearance?
answer: General forbearance is usually granted for up to a year at a time and can be renewed while your hardship continues. For loans disbursed on or after July 1, 2027, forbearance for reasons like poor health or other hardship is limited to nine months in any 24-month period. Interest keeps accruing during forbearance on every loan type, so it can make your balance grow. Ask your servicer whether switching plans would work better than pausing.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.205 (eCFR)
sources.section: General forbearance; duration; loans disbursed on or after July 1, 2027

question: Do I have to apply to defer my loans while I'm in school?
answer: Usually not. In-school deferment is an exception to the general rule that you have to request a deferment: it's typically processed automatically from the enrollment information your school reports, as long as you're enrolled at least half-time. If your servicer bills you even though you're enrolled, ask your school to confirm your enrollment was reported, and contact your servicer. Parent PLUS borrowers are different and have to request their deferment.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.204 (eCFR)
sources.section: In-school deferment; requesting deferments; (c) Direct PLUS

question: Going into the Peace Corps after graduation. Do my loans have to be paid while I'm serving?
answer: Peace Corps service is one of the ways to qualify for an economic hardship deferment, which can cover your service term up to the deferment's three-year limit. That deferment isn't available for newer loans disbursed after the cutoff set by recent law, so check which of your loans qualify. Interest still accrues on unsubsidized loans during a deferment. Contact your servicer before you leave to set it up.

question: Is it smart to just keep my loans in forbearance until I make more money?
answer: It can be costly. Interest keeps adding up on every loan during forbearance, so your balance can grow while you aren't paying. An income-driven plan such as the Repayment Assistance Plan sets your payment based on your income, and on RAP, unpaid interest is waived when you make on-time payments. Ask your servicer to compare your options before you choose a long forbearance.

sources.title: Student Loan Repayment Checklist (Federal Student Aid, PDF)
sources.section: If you can't make a payment

question: How does Public Service Loan Forgiveness work?
answer: PSLF forgives the remaining balance on your Direct Loans after you make 120 qualifying monthly payments while working full-time for a qualifying employer, such as a government agency or a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Payments must be made under a qualifying plan, such as an income-driven plan, RAP or the 10-year standard plan, and you can't be in default when you apply. You have to be working for a qualifying employer when you apply and when your last qualifying payment is made. Submit your employment certification through StudentAid.gov to track your progress.

question: Do RAP payments count toward PSLF?
answer: Yes. The Department's regulations say repaying under the Repayment Assistance Plan counts as a qualifying repayment plan for PSLF, as long as you meet all the other requirements: Direct Loans, full-time work for a qualifying employer, and 120 qualifying payments. If you're switching from SAVE or another plan, choosing RAP or another income-driven plan keeps you on a PSLF-qualifying plan.

sources.title: Reimagining and Improving Student Education; Federal Student Loan Program Final Regulations (Federal Register, May 1, 2026)

question: Will payments on the Tiered Standard plan count for PSLF?
answer: Not necessarily. The PSLF rules count income-driven plans, RAP and the 10-year standard plan, and other plans only when the monthly payment is at least what you'd pay on a 10-year standard plan. A Tiered Standard plan with a longer term usually has a lower payment than that, so those payments may not count. If you're pursuing PSLF, ask your servicer before choosing a Tiered Standard plan; RAP is the safer choice for PSLF.

question: I heard some nonprofits won't count for PSLF anymore. Is that true?
answer: The Department published a rule that would exclude employers it finds have a "substantial illegal purpose," such as supporting terrorism or a pattern of aiding illegal discrimination, for activities on or after July 1, 2026, and it still appears in the federal regulations. The rule has been challenged in federal court, so whether and how it applies is uncertain right now. Check the PSLF information on StudentAid.gov for the current status before you make job decisions based on it.

question: does part time work count for pslf if i have two jobs?
answer: PSLF requires full-time employment, which generally means averaging at least 30 hours a week. The rules count qualifying employment in one or more jobs, so two qualifying jobs can add up to full-time. Each employer has to be a qualifying employer and certify your employment. Use the PSLF tools in your StudentAid.gov account to submit the certifications.

question: What does consolidating my federal loans actually do?
answer: A Direct Consolidation Loan combines your federal education loans into one new loan with one payment and one servicer, and the old loans are paid off. The interest rate is the weighted average of the rates on the loans you consolidate, rounded up to the nearest one-eighth of a percentage point, so consolidating doesn't lower your rate. It can make some loans eligible for plans or forgiveness programs they wouldn't otherwise qualify for. Apply through StudentAid.gov, and compare the effect on your repayment plan options first.

question: If I consolidate, do I lose the payments I've already made toward PSLF?
answer: Not entirely. Under current PSLF rules, qualifying payments you made before consolidating count toward the new consolidation loan on a weighted-average basis, based on how much of the new loan each old loan makes up. That means a loan with fewer payments can pull the average down. Check your payment counts in your StudentAid.gov account before you consolidate.

question: Can I consolidate while I'm still in my grace period?
answer: Yes. Borrowers in the grace period are eligible to apply for a Direct Consolidation Loan. You can apply on StudentAid.gov.

question: Whats the difference between being delinquent and being in default?
answer: You're delinquent as soon as you miss a payment, and you may be charged late fees. A Direct Loan goes into default after you fail to make payments for 270 days. Default is much more serious: the whole unpaid balance and interest can become due at once, and the default is reported to credit agencies. If you've missed payments, contact your servicer right away about changing plans, deferment or forbearance.

sources.title: Student Loan Repayment Checklist (Federal Student Aid, PDF)
U.S. Department of Education Delays Involuntary Collections Amid Ongoing Student Loan Repayment Improvements

question: What actually happens to me if my student loans go into default?
answer: Once a federal loan defaults, the entire unpaid balance and interest can become due immediately, and the default is reported to credit bureaus, which can hurt your credit. The government can also use involuntary collection, such as taking your federal tax refund through the Treasury Offset Program or garnishing wages, though the Department has paused and restarted these at different times. Getting out of default through rehabilitation or consolidation stops this. Contact your defaulted loan servicer to start.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Education Delays Involuntary Collections Amid Ongoing Student Loan Repayment Improvements
GEN-25-19: Request for Institutions to Provide Repayment Information to Former Students to Prevent Defaults

question: Are they really collecting on defaulted student loans again?
answer: Yes, collections restarted. On May 5, 2025, the Department of Education resumed collections on its defaulted loan portfolio, starting with the Treasury Offset Program, which can take federal payments like tax refunds, and said wage garnishment would follow. In January 2026 the Department announced a temporary delay of wage garnishment and Treasury offset while it put new repayment reforms in place, without giving an end date. This status can change, so if you're in default, contact your defaulted loan servicer now about rehabilitation or consolidation.

sources.title: GEN-25-19: Request for Institutions to Provide Repayment Information to Former Students to Prevent Defaults
U.S. Department of Education Delays Involuntary Collections Amid Ongoing Student Loan Repayment Improvements

question: How do I get my loan out of default with rehabilitation?
answer: To rehabilitate a defaulted Direct Loan, you agree to a monthly payment based on your income and make nine voluntary, on-time payments, each within 20 days of the due date, over 10 consecutive months. Once you finish, the loan goes back into regular repayment and the Department asks credit agencies to remove the record of the default from your credit history. Contact your defaulted loan servicer to request a rehabilitation agreement.

question: I rehabbed a loan years ago and it defaulted again. Can I rehabilitate it a second time?
answer: Usually not yet. Under current rules a loan can be rehabilitated only once, so a loan that defaulted again after an earlier rehabilitation generally can't be rehabilitated a second time. A rule change allows a second rehabilitation, but only for loans that default on or after July 1, 2027, and it also raises the minimum rehabilitation payment from $5 to $10 a month. For a loan that's in default now, ask your defaulted loan servicer about other ways out, such as consolidation.

sources.title: Reimagining and Improving Student Education; Federal Student Loan Program Final Regulations (Federal Register, May 1, 2026)

question: Is consolidation another way to get out of default?
answer: Yes. You can consolidate a defaulted loan into a new Direct Consolidation Loan if you make satisfactory repayment arrangements first or agree to repay the new loan under an income-driven plan. Rehabilitation is the route the rules tie to removing the default from your credit history, so ask about both before you choose. Your defaulted loan servicer can explain the requirements, and you can apply on StudentAid.gov.

question: how do i find out who my loan servicer is and how much i owe?
answer: Log in to your account on StudentAid.gov. It lists each of your federal loans with its balance, interest rate, loan type and the name of its servicer. Most people have one servicer, but you can have more than one. Make an online account with your servicer and keep your contact information up to date so you don't miss notices.

sources.title: Student Loan Repayment Checklist (Federal Student Aid, PDF)
sources.section: Find your loans and your servicer

question: Do I have to pay a company to help me manage my federal student loans?
answer: No. Your federal loan servicer handles billing, repayment plan changes, deferment and forbearance at no cost to you. Everything a paid company would do for you, like applying for RAP or IBR or consolidating, you can do yourself free through StudentAid.gov or your servicer. Be careful with anyone who charges fees for these services.

sources.title: Student Loan Repayment Checklist (Federal Student Aid, PDF)

question: I can't afford my student loan payment this month. What should I do?
answer: Contact your servicer right away, before you miss the payment if you can. Ask about switching to an income-based plan such as the Repayment Assistance Plan or, for older loans, IBR, which can lower your payment, or about deferment or forbearance if you need a short break. Missing even one payment makes the loan delinquent and may bring late fees, so getting ahead of it matters.

sources.title: Student Loan Repayment Checklist (Federal Student Aid, PDF)
sources.section: If you can't make a payment

question: Can my student loans be forgiven if I become disabled?
answer: Yes, through a Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge. You can qualify with a VA finding that you're unemployable because of a service-connected disability, with Social Security Administration documentation of disability benefits that meet the rules, or with certification from a physician, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or licensed psychologist. The Department may also discharge loans automatically based on VA or SSA data. If you take out a new federal loan within three years after the discharge, the old debt can be reinstated.

question: My school shut down in the middle of my program. Do I still owe my loans?
answer: You may qualify for a closed school discharge if you were enrolled when the school closed or withdrew no more than 180 days before it closed, and you didn't finish your program at another location of the school or through a teach-out at another school. In some cases the Department discharges eligible loans automatically one year after the closure. Apply through StudentAid.gov or contact your servicer.

question: My for-profit college lied about job placement. Is there a way to get my loans cancelled?
answer: You can apply for borrower defense to repayment, which can cancel federal loans when a school misled students or engaged in certain misconduct related to the loans or the education. Depending on when your loans were disbursed, you may need to show the school made a misrepresentation that you relied on and that it caused you financial harm. The Department of Education reviews the application and decides. Apply on StudentAid.gov, and keep any evidence like ads, emails or enrollment documents.

question: I work for a nonprofit hospital. Can you promise my loans will be forgiven through PSLF in 10 years?
answer: I can't promise that, because the Department of Education decides PSLF eligibility based on your employer, your loans, your plan and each payment. In general you need Direct Loans, full-time work for a qualifying employer such as a 501(c)(3), and 120 qualifying payments under a qualifying plan, and you can't be in default when you apply. Certify your employment regularly through StudentAid.gov so you can see your count and fix problems early.

question: Just tell me, will RAP or IBR give me the lower payment?
answer: I can't tell you which is lower for you without your income, family size and loans, and even then your servicer's calculation is what counts. In general, RAP charges a share of your adjusted gross income that rises as your income rises, minus a set amount for each dependent, with a small minimum payment, while IBR is based on your discretionary income and is only available for loans made before the new rules took effect. Compare estimates in your StudentAid.gov account or ask your servicer to calculate both before you switch.

sources.title: 34 CFR 685.209 (eCFR)
sources.section: RAP and IBR payment calculations; (d)(5) IBR eligibility

question: Can I list my roommate's kids as my dependents on my RAP application so my payment goes down?
answer: No. For RAP, a dependent is someone who qualifies as your dependent under the tax code and whom you actually claimed on your federal tax return, so the plan relies on the same information as your return. Listing people who don't meet that definition would be false information on a federal application. If your payment is too high, ask your servicer about your real options, such as deferment, forbearance or a different plan.

question: If I rehab my defaulted loan, can you guarantee my credit score goes back to normal?
answer: No one can guarantee what happens to your credit score. The rule is that once you complete rehabilitation, the Department asks credit agencies to remove the record of the default from your credit history, but your score depends on your whole credit history. Your defaulted loan servicer can explain what will be reported.

question: What's my exact deadline to get off SAVE?
answer: I can't see your account, so I can't tell you your date. The Department said servicers would send each SAVE borrower a notice with their own deadline, giving at least 90 days to choose a new plan. Check the notice from your servicer or log in to your StudentAid.gov account, and remember you can switch any time before the deadline.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Education Announces Next Steps for Borrowers Enrolled in the Unlawful SAVE Plan
